title: Hearing Charlie Parker, Wallace Allen, the Bebop Jockers and the Johnson Brothers
summary: Ford first heard Parker on Jazz at the Philharmonic, sat in for Harold Dejan at the Opera House, played in Wallace Allen's Bebop Jockers, then joined the Johnson Brothers and made 'Mellow Mama' for Deluxe.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: All 78's, I don't remember seeing it. If there was, I believe, Jazz to Philharmonic was the first LP I saw. And that's where I first heard Charlie Park on him. He played Lady Be Good and I said yeah that's the saxophone play I wanted. Well I really first heard him when I was graduating from high school, because Wallace, Wallace Allen was in my class, he and I graduated together. Was he in the band? No. Wallace was, well he was a man when I was a kid because he had been in the Navy band. Oh yeah. And the band was sort of like a step down for him. He was playing, he had his own band at the Dewdrop at the time. But after I left with Joe Jones, Joe Jones was graduating from high school, the next band step for me was Wallace. We went back to school again and we took up Short Hand, Typing and Geek. This was in 48, I remember this very well. And Wallace was in the class and Wallace was playing with Harold DeJong at the Opera House. Opera House. Uh huh. And we had been, he said, he told me, he said Harold needed someone to play in his place. And he said, well, do you think he could make it? I said, I don't know. So he said, come out and try. So I went and played with him that night. And of course I had been listening to these Charlie Parker records that I had bought from this shop. And they were playing, one or two of them they played with Salt Peanuts at the time, getting into the bebop thing. And Harold said, I'll never forget, he said, that must be a CG Conn you're playing on, because that's what he still talks about. And I said, yeah, that's what it is. And we played and he said, the next night he took off and I played and I made ten dollars, which was very good for that time. Because I used to give my mother half of what I made and I'd keep half and I still had good money. I made five dollars, but it would last me a week. See. And so I played, Wallace got a little band together and we called it the Bebop, that's in this book here. Oh yeah, the Bebop. The Bebop Jockers, yeah, I remember. The Bebop Jockers, we never made a dime. I believe the best thing we had, we worked Bourbon Street for three weeks. And that band made, I believe it made 60 dollars a week, which was good, I believe it was 1949, it was before I got married in 1949. We made 60 dollars a week for three weeks. And that was very, very good money. And we played the band a while and I believe Wallace, we couldn't find out what we couldn't find any work. And the next band, one of them was the Johnson Brothers, they called me. Johnson Brothers. Yeah, Johnson Brothers. And this was 49 also, the end of 49. And I worked with them. They had a band that was very popular. They played dances. They played six nights a week, different places. Plas Johnson is right now in Hollywood, he plays tenor. He's the brother who's the most famous. He's most famous for the Pink Panther. You ever hear that? The comedy, the saxophone solo, that's Plas. That's him. He was playing like that then, the same way. He played tenor. I was playing alto sax and they had a five piece band and they wanted an alto sax, because they were going to make a record. And I think that's the first record I made called Mellow Mama. What's that? We made it at Booker T. Washington, Booker T. Washington Auditorium. They brought these things, you like this. Yeah. And Paul Gaten supervised it. Oh, for what? I couldn't tell you. Oh wait, yes I can too. Deluxe.
Deluxe. I believe Deluxe had another company that they- Regal, was that?
Well, it was Deluxe. I tell you. Yeah, because, well that was the company.
